1How to read every number in this document

This document is the answer sheet to the modelling setup: the same sections, now with their outcomes. Every score is a subject-level AUC under leave-one-subject-out validation, one averaged probability per person, exactly as the protocol defined it.

The other scores used in this document

One later section cuts each model’s probabilities at a threshold and reports the resulting decisions, counted in four cells. With PD as the positive class: TP is a PD subject correctly called, TN a control correctly left alone, FP a control wrongly flagged, FN a PD subject missed. Every further score is arithmetic on those four counts:

ScoreFormulaPlain meaning
Recall (sensitivity)TP / (TP + FN)the share of true PD subjects the model catches
SpecificityTN / (TN + FP)the share of true controls correctly left unflagged
PrecisionTP / (TP + FP)when the model says PD, how often it is right
F12 · precision · recall / (precision + recall)one number balancing catching PD and being right when flagging
Balanced accuracy(recall + specificity) / 2the average hit rate across the two classes

The floors

Two deliberately impoverished predictors were scored under the identical protocol. They are the floors: any model not clearly above them has demonstrated nothing about gait.

FloorAUCWhat it is
Recording duration alone0.610 One number per subject, how long their recordings last, fed to a logistic regression under the same leave-one-subject-out loop. This is the classical grid’s own duration_only cell; no gait content at all.
Window count alone0.620 No model at all: subjects are ranked directly by how many windows they yield (a restatement of duration) and the AUC of that ranking is computed.

How every result is judged

The same two readings accompany every result in this document, so they are defined once here and never re-introduced.

ReadingHow it is computedWhat it answers
Pooled AUC All 58 subject scores against the 58 diagnoses. The headline number, comparable to the literature.
95 % confidence interval The 58 subjects are redrawn with replacement 2,000 times (some subjects appearing twice, others not at all), the AUC recomputed each time, and the interval is the middle 95 % of those 2,000 values. The error bar on the score: the range the score would most likely stay inside if the whole study were repeated with a different set of 58 people. If 0.5 sits inside that range, the score cannot be trusted to beat a coin flip.
Key point

The finding, stated up front. The campaign was built to answer one question: does this dataset carry a gait signature that models can read? No such signature was demonstrable: pooled scores sit between 0.56 and 0.69, every 95 % confidence interval contains the duration floor of 0.610, and the interpretability experiments attribute what score there is to properties of the recordings rather than of the walks. This is a statement about the signal in the data, not about the models: they behaved exactly as models should, finding the strongest pattern available, and that pattern was not gait. Establishing this rigorously, where the literature would have reported the 0.69 as a success, is the contribution. The rest of this document is the evidence.

2The classical yardstick, measured

The setup promised a 15-cell grid: three classifiers, logistic regression, an SVM and a random forest, by five feature sets, each cell a full leave-one-subject-out run over the 58 subjects.

Modelall_featuresduration_invariantshape_cleanconfounded_onlyduration_only
logreg0.6330.6270.6210.6750.610
SVM0.6230.6010.5770.6340.287
random_forest0.6050.6010.5830.6180.450
The five feature sets, in one line each
SetWhat it contains
all_featuresAll 25 handcrafted measurements, no restraint.
duration_invariantOnly measurements whose definition cannot grow with recording length (averages, shapes, ratios; no totals).
shape_cleanThe subset of those that also pass a direct test against measured duration: the cleanest description of the walk’s shape.
confounded_onlyOnly the totals, which grow with recording length.
duration_onlyRecording length and nothing else: the floor.
Key point

Read the logistic regression row right to left. Its duration_only cell, recording length alone, scores 0.610. Its confounded_only cell, the measurements that merely encode length, scores 0.675, the best cell in the table. Its shape_clean cell, the measurements describing the shape of the walk with length removed, scores 0.621. The further the features get from elapsed time, the worse the classifier does: the grid is the controlled experiment the setup designed, and it came out in the direction that indicts the confound.

The confidence intervals, applied to the grid

Section 1 defined the interval that accompanies every result. Applied to the grid, it says which of its numbers is real: the interval on the confounded cell runs from 0.527 to 0.813 and excludes 0.5, so the length signal is genuinely there; the interval on the clean cell runs from 0.473 to 0.770 and contains 0.5, so the gait signal has not been shown to exist.

4Decisions, not just rankings

Every score so far has been an AUC, and an AUC measures ranking: the probability that a randomly drawn PD subject scores above a randomly drawn control. A screening deployment cannot rank, it must decide, and a decision needs a threshold. As pre-registered, each headline model's per-subject probabilities are cut at the prevalence of the positive class, 25/58 = 0.431: any subject scoring at or above it is called PD. This section reports what the four headline models decide at that threshold, for all 58 subjects.

ModelRecall (sensitivity)SpecificityPrecisionF1Balanced accuracy
Classical logistic regression0.680.550.530.600.61
SmallCNN0.600.670.580.590.63
ResNet-18 probe0.680.480.500.580.58
Envelope-LSTM0.600.640.560.580.62
Key point

The honest reading of this section. At the pre-registered threshold the best deep model catches 17 of the 25 PD subjects and misses 8, while falsely flagging 17 of the 33 controls; balanced accuracy across the four models spans 0.58 to 0.63. These are roughly the catch-and-miss numbers a deployment would see, and they are exactly consistent with the AUC story: near-chance discrimination looks, at decision time, like a coin that is only slightly bent.

5What the models attended to

Every number so far says how well the models scored. This section asks where they were looking when they scored, using Grad-CAM: for a given window, the gradient of the model’s PD output with respect to its last convolutional layer says which regions of the picture pushed the decision, and the weighted, rectified sum of those activations is drawn over the spectrogram as a heat map. This is the direct check the field’s own cautionary tale demands, the test that would have caught the published network reading its recording sites. It was run on all 58 folds of both deep models, one map per window of each held-out subject.

Caution

A caveat that belongs in the report: the maps are max-normalised per window, so comparisons between windows describe how attention is distributed, not the raw strength of the underlying output. The band and turn comparisons above are distribution statements, and are read as such.

Key point

The interpretability finding in one sentence: the models were not looking at the walk. Attention concentrates on the background rows above 500 Hz and on the turn segments, PD-labelled windows carry more background attention than control windows (mass 0.33 against 0.27, centre of attention 380 Hz against 333 Hz), and the gait bands are the least-attended part of the picture. The attention maps independently corroborate that the scores measure properties of the recordings, not of the walks.

6Suppressing what they attended to: the follow-up experiment

The attention maps point at a specific, removable channel, so they were put to work. A follow-up experiment, pre-registered in its own configuration file before any window was rebuilt, changes exactly two things about the input and nothing else: each recording’s background profile (its per-frequency median over time) is subtracted before windowing, and the empty rows beyond ±500 Hz are cropped away, so the region the attention maps flooded no longer exists. Both deep models were then re-run under the full, unchanged protocol.

ModelPooled AUC95 % CI
SmallCNN, background-suppressed0.624[0.471, 0.768]
SmallCNN, standard input (reference)0.616[0.468, 0.760]
ResNet-18 probe, background-suppressed0.686[0.539, 0.824]
ResNet-18 probe, standard input (reference)0.654[0.509, 0.798]

Two readings:

  • The scores did not collapse. Both models hold or slightly exceed their reference values with the background gone, the confidence intervals overlapping almost entirely. The recording-level nuisance therefore leaks through more channels than the visible texture: removing the region the attention flooded still leaves enough per-recording signature, plausibly in the in-band enhancement characteristics, for the models to find. The nuisance is not one removable feature; it is a property of the per-recording processing.
  • No hidden gait signal surfaced. If the background texture had been masking a true gait signal, removing it should have lifted the scores clearly above the duration floor. Instead every interval still contains 0.610, so the experiment uncovered nothing gait-shaped underneath.
Key point

The follow-up strengthens the finding either way it could have gone, and it went the confirming way: the negative result stands after the attention-guided intervention, and the experiment adds a mechanistic detail the campaign alone could not: the per-recording nuisance is distributed through the recording, not confined to the background the models preferred to read.

7Verdict, and what stays open

Key point

The verdict. Under leak-free, subject-independent validation, no model family and no configuration clearly exceeds the recording-duration floor on this dataset: every confidence interval contains 0.610, the attention maps show the models reading per-recording texture and turn segments rather than the gait bands, and removing that texture leaves the scores unchanged. The one signal that survives every control is the clinically real observation that PD subjects take longer, carried by elapsed time, not by the spectral shape of the walk. This outcome was pre-registered as a possibility before the first model ran, and together with the random-split demonstration it shows how apparent radar-PD performance can be manufactured by validation design and per-recording nuisances.

Key point

A statement the report must carry: eleven deep configurations were explored in total across the campaign and its exploratory variants; the informative ones are shown in this document and every run is archived, so nothing was selected for looking good. With 58 subjects, quoting only the best of eleven runs would manufacture exactly the optimism this thesis criticises. The best first-pass number (0.674) is stated with the pre-registered re-test that brought it back down.

Caution

One discovery is about the data rather than the models: under the background-corrected direction labels, 24 of the 58 subjects have no window with a clean single-direction foot signature, in an all-or-nothing pattern per subject, consistent with a per-recording sign convention in how the two foot radars were merged. It is a standing question for the data owners and it gates the one untried signal source: left/right asymmetry, which needs the per-node arrays.

Still openWhat it would settle
The formal confound batteryHeadline models re-scored duration-matched and on the chair-free variant only.
The two recording sessionsThe corpus shows signs of having been captured in two sessions with different PD shares. Whether that matters, and how to treat it, is a question for the supervisor and the data owners; session-restricted analyses are archived outside this document pending that conversation.
Subject agesWhether even the duration signal is disease or ageing.
The random-split demonstrationAlready run; it opens the discussion chapter and shows the same model posting literature-grade numbers the moment the protocol is relaxed.
